name: Cinnamon / apple cider vinegar shots
lead: Cinnamon and apple cider vinegar (ACV) shots are a home-made drink in which diluted apple cider vinegar, sometimes with cinnamon, is swallowed in the hope of a leaner midsection, less bloating and clearer skin. Practitioners use it as a daily morning or pre-meal routine, on the reasoning that vinegar and cinnamon blunt blood-sugar spikes and appetite, which in turn supports fat loss and a leaner look.[1][2]

Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting pressed apple juice first to alcohol and then to acetic acid; it is about 94% water and 5% acetic acid, with 22 kcal per 100 g.[1] Cinnamon is the bark of Cinnamomum trees; most commercial cinnamon is cassia, while Ceylon (true) cinnamon comes mainly from Sri Lanka.[2]

Research on the two ingredients is mostly about metabolic markers rather than appearance. Wikipedia reports no high-quality clinical evidence that regular vinegar use helps with body weight or blood glucose and lipids, and that major public-health organizations do not recommend it as a therapy.[1] For cinnamon, a 2012 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for diabetes, while a 2023 meta-analysis of meta-analyses reported modest reductions in fasting glucose and HbA1c.[2]

angle.text: People take diluted ACV shots, sometimes with cinnamon, expecting less bloating and appetite so they can stay lean and look slimmer through the midsection. Some also say it improves skin.

paras: A shot generally means a small amount of vinegar diluted in water, with cinnamon added in some recipes. Apple cider vinegar is made by yeast fermentation of apple juice to cider, followed by acetic acid bacteria (Acetobacter) converting the alcohol to acetic acid; unfiltered versions may keep a cellulose "mother" biofilm.[1] It has long been used in dressings, marinades and preserves, and recipes for it appear in 19th-century cookbooks.[1]

Claimed benefits include weight loss, reduced bloating, blood sugar and cholesterol control, and improved skin.[1] Cinnamon is added for flavour and for claimed effects on blood sugar and appetite, a link examined mainly in people with diabetes.[2][3]

Cassia cinnamon contains more coumarin than Ceylon cinnamon, a compound that can affect the liver at high intakes. EFSA set a tolerable daily intake of 0.1 mg per kg body weight in 2008, equal to roughly 0.4 g of high-coumarin cassia per day for a 50 kg adult.[2] Reported side effects of cinnamon are mainly gastrointestinal upset and allergic reactions.[2]

For vinegar, Wikipedia cites a 2020 systematic review in the European Journal of Nutrition on safety, side effects, metabolic parameters and body weight, and says no high-quality evidence shows benefit for body weight or glucose.[1]

For cinnamon, a 2024 updated meta-analysis of randomized trials in type 2 diabetes described the effect on glycemic control as inconclusive, and a 2003 trial of 60 people with type 2 diabetes tested 1, 3 or 6 g of cinnamon daily against placebo, titled as improving glucose and lipids.[3][4] A 2024 four-week crossover trial examined cinnamon and continuously monitored glucose response in adults with prediabetes.[5] No published trials were found of the combined vinegar-and-cinnamon shot for appearance or skin.

Wikipedia lists tooth-enamel damage from large quantities, esophageal damage from incompletely swallowed tablets, more burping and flatulence, increased tooth sensitivity, possible interactions with insulin or diuretics, and possible allergy in people with apple allergy; topical use on skin may cause burns.[1] Moderate, diluted consumption was considered low-risk in the 2020 review.[1]

timeline.event: An English cookbook by Esther Copley includes an apple cider vinegar recipe.[1]
A randomized trial of cinnamon capsules in 60 people with type 2 diabetes is published in Diabetes Care.[4]
EFSA sets a tolerable daily intake for coumarin of 0.1 mg per kg body weight.[2]
A Cochrane review finds insufficient evidence for cinnamon in diabetes.[2]
A systematic review examines vinegar safety, metabolic parameters and body weight.[1]

card.summary: Diluted apple cider vinegar (sometimes with cinnamon) taken for fat loss and skin; no high-quality trials back the appearance claims.
card.note: Undiluted or excessive vinegar is reported to damage tooth enamel and irritate the throat.

quick.overview:
ACV shots are small servings of diluted apple cider vinegar, sometimes mixed with cinnamon, drunk in the hope of losing fat, reducing bloating or clearing skin.

Wikipedia reports no high-quality clinical evidence that regular use affects body weight or blood sugar and lipids, and that health organizations do not recommend it as a therapy.
quick.mechanism: Proponents attribute effects to acetic acid, which they say curbs appetite and moderates blood sugar. Published high-quality evidence for these effects in appearance terms was not found.
quick.risks: Diluted moderate use is generally described as low-risk. Reported harms include tooth-enamel erosion, throat and esophageal irritation, digestive upset, and burns when applied to skin or eyes. Possible interactions with insulin and diuretics are noted.
